lessons.title: Why Defensives Hold Up: Staples, Pricing Power, and Repeat Demand

body.text: A true defensive is built on three things working together: people buy it every week no matter what, the company can raise prices without losing those buyers, and the business needs very little capital to run. Remove any one of the three and the defence starts to crack.

children.text: Chapter 2 took apart the machinery that makes cyclical profits swing. This chapter does the same for defensives. The goal is not to admire them. It is to understand exactly what protects their earnings, so you can tell a genuinely defensive business from one that merely sells everyday products, and spot when the protection is weakening.
What Defensive Earnings Actually Look Like

body.caption: Hindustan Unilever consolidated, ₹ crore (source: Screener.in annual figures)

children.text: Put this next to Tata Steel's table from the last lesson. Over FY15 to FY25, HUL's net profit fell in just one year, by 5.1% in FY16, and grew at about 9.3% a year compounded. FY21, the lockdown year, delivered 18.4% profit growth, helped by the merger of GSK Consumer Healthcare's India business, which took effect in April 2020. Its operating margin never moved more than two percentage points in a single year.

body.text: Run the Chapter 1 scorecard on these two and you hit a quirk: the coefficient of variation of net profit is 0.33 for HUL and 0.32 for Colgate, just above the 0.3 defensive cut-off. That is not volatility. A company whose profit steadily doubles over a decade has a wide spread of values simply because it grew. For consistently growing businesses, give more weight to loss years, decline years, and the size of the worst decline, which here read clearly defensive.

markDefs.definition: Switching to smaller packs, cheaper variants, or lower-priced brands within the same category when household budgets are squeezed, rather than stopping purchases altogether.

children.text: Toothpaste, soap, detergent, tea, and biscuits are bought every week or month, cost a small slice of a household budget, and cannot be postponed the way a car or a flat can. When incomes are squeezed, families do not stop buying them. They engage in

: a ₹10 sachet instead of a large bottle, a value brand instead of a premium one. That shows up as slower volume growth or a weaker product mix, not a collapse in sales. Compare that with a truck buyer, who can simply skip a year.

columns.label: At a staples company
points: Volume growth slows from high single digits to low single digits
Customers shift to smaller packs and value variants
Margins dip by a point or two, profit growth slows

columns.label: At a steel or auto company
points: Dealer or plant inventory builds up, forcing production cuts
Margins fall many points, profit can turn into a loss

children.text: Stable demand alone is not enough, as telecom showed in Chapter 1. What protects a staples company's margins is the ability to pass on cost increases. Strong brands, wide distribution, and habit let leaders raise prices when palm oil, crude-linked packaging, or milk costs jump. The FY22 to FY23 inflation shock is the clearest recent test. HUL's OPM dipped from 25% in FY22 to 23% in FY23 and profit still grew 14.1%. In the same year, Tata Steel's consolidated OPM fell from 26% to 13%. Both faced higher input costs. Only one could pass them on.

In India, pricing power often works quietly. Popular price points like ₹5, ₹10, and ₹20 are sacred for small packs, because shoppers and shopkeepers are used to them. So instead of raising the price, companies reduce the grams in the pack. The rupee price stays the same; the price per gram rises.

body.title: Protect the ₹10 Price Point
body.prompt: A detergent sachet sells for ₹10 and contains 80 grams. Raw material costs per gram rise 20%. To keep the raw material cost of each sachet unchanged without touching the ₹10 price, how many grams should the new sachet contain? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Cost per gram is now 1.2 times the old level, so grams must fall to 80 ÷ 1.2 = 66.7 grams. The shopper still pays ₹10, but the effective price per gram has risen 20%. Only a brand strong enough to keep buyers from switching can do this repeatedly.

markDefs.definition: Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days. It shows how long a company's cash is tied up in operations; a negative number means suppliers and distributors are effectively funding the business.

children.text: The third pillar is the one most investors overlook. Leading staples companies need relatively little capital: factories are modest compared with a steel plant, and many sell to distributors who pay quickly while buying from suppliers on credit. That can push the

below zero. The result is high returns on capital and little need to borrow, which means almost no fixed costs or interest to magnify a downturn. Remember DOL and DFL from Chapter 2: defensives keep both close to their minimum.

body.title: Who Funds the Business?
body.textWithBlank: When a company collects cash from distributors before it has to pay its own suppliers, it has a ___ cash conversion cycle.
body.explanation: A negative cash conversion cycle means suppliers are effectively financing the company's operations. Growth does not require borrowing, which keeps financial leverage and interest costs low.

body.title: Spot the Weak Pillar
body.question: Which of these features does NOT make a staples company more defensive?
options: Products bought every week at low price points
A brand strong enough to cut grammage without losing customers
A negative cash conversion cycle and no borrowings
Rapid sales growth funded by heavy borrowing and deep discounts
body.explanation: Debt-funded, discount-driven growth adds financial leverage and shows weak pricing power, which is the opposite of what protects earnings in a downturn. The first three options are the three pillars.

body.title: Is It Really Defensive?
body.scenario: Rohit, a salaried professional who invests through Zerodha, wants to add a defensive stock before what he expects to be a slowdown. He shortlists a recently listed personal care company. Sales have grown 45% a year for three years and its shampoos sell well online. But it has reported losses every year, spends over 30% of sales on marketing, and says it plans to turn profitable in two years. Rohit reasons that shampoo is an everyday product, so the stock must be defensive.
body.prompt: Does Rohit's shortlist pass the three-pillar test? What would you tell him?
body.modelAnswer: It fails at least two of the three pillars. Demand for shampoo is repeat, but this company's customers may not be loyal yet: heavy marketing spend suggests it is buying growth rather than enjoying pricing power. It has no profit history, so there is no evidence of how its earnings behave in a slowdown. And a loss-making business burning cash may need to raise more capital or borrow, possibly at a bad time. In a downturn, loss-making growth companies often face funding pressure and sharp derating, which is not defensive behaviour. The category is defensive; this company is not, at least not yet. For defensive exposure, Rohit should look for businesses with a long record of profits through past slowdowns, stable margins, and little or no debt.

body.title: Three-Pillar Check on Screener.in
steps: Profit and Loss: count loss years and profit decline years, and note the worst decline, over 10 years
Profit and Loss: check that OPM moved within a narrow band, especially in FY22 and FY23 when input costs surged
Profit and Loss: check FY20 and FY21 for how earnings held up through the pandemic
Balance Sheet: confirm borrowings are minimal relative to annual profit
Ratios: look for consistently high ROCE and low or negative cash conversion cycle days
Annual report or earnings calls: look for evidence of price increases or grammage changes that did not cost market share
Write down which of the three pillars is strongest and which is weakest

points: True defensives rest on three pillars: repeat low-ticket demand, pricing power, and light capital with little debt
HUL's net profit fell in only one year between FY15 and FY25 and compounded at about 9.3% a year
In a slowdown, staples customers down-trade to smaller packs and cheaper variants instead of stopping purchases
Pricing power, not stable demand alone, protects margins; in FY23 HUL's OPM dipped two points while Tata Steel's halved
Grammage cuts at fixed price points like ₹10 are a common way Indian FMCG companies pass on costs
Low capital needs and negative working capital keep operating and financial leverage low
For steadily growing companies, the coefficient of variation overstates volatility, so weight decline years and worst decline more heavily

body.text: HUL and Colgate-Palmolive India figures are annual data as displayed on Screener.in at the time of writing and may be restated. FY25 is used as HUL's end year because later figures include large non-operating income. The sachet example, the business types table, and Rohit's scenario are illustrative. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
